claims.text: Local chemical short-range order induces spatial fluctuations in shear-fault energy in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Shear-fault-energy fluctuations dominate dislocation pinning and strengthening in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Shear-fault-energy fluctuations govern deformation behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys.
A homogenized CrCoNi or NiCoCr alloy can have minimal detectable SRO and predominantly random chemical mixing.
Heat treatment can promote L12-type SRO relative to L11-type SRO in CrCoNi nanoclusters.
Promoting L12-type ordering relative to L11-type ordering increases local shear-fault-energy fluctuations.
SRO nanoclusters locally modulate shear-fault energy and create heterogeneous energy landscapes on slip planes.
Larger spatial fluctuations in shear-fault energy produce local hard atomic motifs.
Local hard atomic motifs pin dislocations.
SRO and local fault-energy fluctuations cause wavy or irregular dislocation motion.
Heat-treated alloy with promoted SRO will have higher yield strength than the homogenized baseline.
Heat-treated alloy with promoted SRO will show more irregular, pinned, or wavy dislocation configurations than the baseline.
The homogenized baseline has a more uniform shear-fault-energy distribution than the SRO-promoted state.
The proposed mechanism applies when the alloy remains single phase, second-phase formation is negligible, and dislocation-based plasticity predominates.
Electron diffraction and atom-probe tomography can characterize SRO in CrCoNi.
The quantitative strength contribution and precise dislocation configurations associated with SRO can vary with composition and heat-treatment parameters.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as predominantly random with minimal detectable SRO, but it is also exemplified as having L11 ordering, and the intervention is framed as a shift from L11 to L12. L11 is itself a form of SRO, so the characterization of the baseline as minimally ordered is ambiguous.

The controlled baseline is alternately called homogenized and 'homogenized (as-cast).' As-cast and homogenized are normally distinct processing states, so the baseline preparation is internally unclear.
